note: Follows the lemma-by-lemma commentary on cowness and universals closely; the inline Sāṃkhya gloss is clumsy but the argument is carried.

errors.english: the karma of what is intended
errors.why: བསམ་པའི་ལས (cetayitvā karma) is the bodily/verbal action performed after having intended, not the object of intention.

note: Faithful rendering of Avalokitavrata's gloss on volition and intended action; only the rendering of cetayitvā karma is loose.
Accurate on the Mahāyāna-as-Buddhavacana argument and the patriarch lineage; names correctly identified.

errors.english: Through the force of excessive conceptual attachment
errors.why: ལྷག་པར་ཞེན་པ is adhyavasāya, conceptual determination, not 'excessive attachment'.

fix.find: Through the force of excessive conceptual attachment

errors.english: Not understanding the opponent's thought, one might formulate an objection
errors.why: It is the other party (གཞན་གྱིས) who, failing to understand the author's intention, raises the objection; the English makes the opponent's thought the thing misunderstood.

fix.find: Not understanding the opponent's thought, one might formulate an objection
fix.replace: Another, not understanding the intention, raises an objection

errors.english: That is to say, does it engage with specific characteristics?
errors.why: The commentary only glosses 'those' as the particulars (does conceptual thought NOT engage with them?); the English inverts the question.

fix.find: That is to say, does it engage with specific characteristics?

errors.english: they engage in practical actions directed at purposeful objects
errors.why: དོན་བྱ་བ་བྱེད་པ is arthakriyā: they act toward objects capable of causal efficacy / fulfilling a purpose.

note: Overall argument on svalakṣaṇa vs. conceptual appearance is recognisable, but key Pramāṇa terms and one speaker/question are mishandled.

errors.english: It is the very engagement of the mind with an entity that, by producing an incompatible cause in the nature of a latent tendency (vasana) habitual imprint or predisposition, causes the mind that perceives the absence of an entity to cut the continuity.
errors.why: The cognition of absence (ergative བློས) cuts off the continuity of the very operation of the cognition of an entity; the English makes the entity-cognition the agent.

fix.find: It is the very engagement of the mind with an entity that, by producing an incompatible cause in the nature of a latent tendency (vasana) habitual imprint or predisposition, causes the mind that perceives the absence of an entity to cut the continuity.
fix.replace: By producing an incompatible cause in the nature of a latent tendency (vāsanā), the mind that perceives the absence of an entity cuts off the continuity of the very operation of the mind that perceives an entity.

errors.english: just as coldness comes from fire at that time
errors.why: Fire and cold is the stock example of incompatibility (cold is removed by fire); 'coldness comes from fire' inverts the example.

note: Usable on the non-coexistence (sahānavasthāna) argument, but the agent of the vāsanā-mechanism is reversed and the fire/cold example garbled.

errors.why: ཤེས་རབ is prajñā, insight/wisdom, not faith.

errors.english:
However many natures svabhāva or causes hetu there may be,
An effect kārya does not arise without them.
errors.why: PV I.3: the effect is a reason with respect to the cause (རྒྱུ་ལ), with as many natures as it is invariably connected to; 'cause' is not a member of a list alongside 'natures'.

fix.find:
However many natures svabhāva or causes hetu there may be,
An effect kārya does not arise without them.
fix.replace:
The effect kārya, which cannot occur without the cause hetu
with however many natures svabhāva, [is a reason for the cause].

errors.english:
The means of valid cognition pramāṇa do not apply to what is absent;
This results in the knowledge of non-existence.
errors.why: PV I.4: the non-operation of the pramāṇas has as its result non-engagement (in behaviour) toward what is absent; 'knowledge of non-existence' belongs to the following line.

fix.find:
The means of valid cognition pramāṇa do not apply to what is absent;
This results in the knowledge of non-existence.
fix.replace:
The non-operation of the means of valid cognition pramāṇa
Has as its result non-engagement with what is absent.

errors.english: And whose rays of light, like those of the "All-Good"
errors.why: The verse says the (Buddha's) rays are all-good (samantabhadra) and radiate everywhere; 'like those of' adds a comparison not in the text.

note: The opening of the Pramāṇavārttika: the prose-ified dedicatory verse is fine, but 'faith' for prajñā and the misconstrued kārikās I.3–4 would mislead a reader on the core logic.
Accurate rendering of the refutation of Sāṃkhya pradhāna, including the guṇa verse and the dilemma on capacity; odd paragraph breaks only.

errors.english: although the object of sound does not have a nature of various conjunctions
errors.why: The sense is that conjunction, the object of the word ['variegated'], is not of a variegated nature; 'object of sound' as subject garbles the argument.

note: Sound treatment of the refutation of the Vaiśeṣika variegated whole and conjunction; one clause muddled.
Precise rendering of the analysis of pakṣadharma, pervasion and the three possible restrictions (eva); technical vocabulary correct.

errors.why: གཞལ་བྱ is prameya, the object of valid cognition, not jñeya.

errors.english: One should not accept (Apoha) exclusion of others as the primary object of sound, because this would be a denial
errors.why: This is the opponent's objection (ཞེ་ན): exclusion should not be accepted as word-meaning because [a cognition] negates it; the English states it as a bare assertion and misreads the reason.

errors.english: refers to things other than (Apoha), such as the sounds themselves
errors.why: 'That' refers to the non-exclusion word[-meaning] etc. (i.e. what the opponent proposes), not to 'the sounds themselves'.
མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ here is adhyavasāya, conceptual determination of an unreal object, not emotional attachment.

note: The apoha discussion is followable, but the opponent's objection is not marked as such, prameya is mislabelled, and a stray 'sentence continues to next page' remark is left in the text.
